scoreNote: Strong (5): disagrees with a clear, well-supported position and then confronts the practical debt objection rather than dodging it, landing on a balanced synthesis; relevant examples throughout.

sentences.text: With tuition high and graduates anxious about work, the advice to study whatever the job market wants can sound like simple common sense.
The claim takes this further, urging that students base their choice of field on the availability of jobs in it.

Job prospects deserve serious thought, but I disagree that they should be the basis of the decision, because a field chosen against one's interests and talents often leads to mediocrity and misery rather than security.

sections.role: Body — Interest and aptitude drive success

sentences.text: First, students tend to excel at what genuinely engages them.
A young woman who loves biology will outwork and outperform a classmate who chose the major only because it seemed employable, and her passion will carry her through the inevitable hard years.
Excellence, not mere enrollment in a popular field, is what ultimately earns good work, and excellence grows from genuine interest far more reliably than from cold calculation.
Interest is what sustains the long, unglamorous hours of practice that real competence quietly requires.
Employers, after all, hire the candidate who is genuinely good, not the one who merely picked a fashionable major.
Choosing a field one finds dull, simply because jobs exist, often produces a mediocre worker in an overcrowded market.

sections.role: Body — The market is a moving target

sentences.text: Moreover, betting one's entire education on today's job market is far riskier than it first appears.
Fields that look secure when a student enrolls can be transformed or automated nearly out of existence by the time she graduates four years later.
Skills that transfer — clear thinking, writing, and problem-solving — outlast any particular industry, and these are cultivated best when a student studies something deeply rather than strategically.
The graduate who trained for a single narrow role may find that role gone the very moment the technology behind it shifts.
Chasing the market can leave a graduate both unhappy and, ironically, unemployed.
The most compelling argument for the claim is practical: degrees are expensive, and a graduate buried in debt cannot afford to be idealistic.
This is a real and serious concern, and it would be irresponsible to tell students to ignore whether a field can support a livelihood.
But acknowledging job prospects as one important factor is very different from making them the basis of the entire choice.
The wiser path is to weigh interest, aptitude, and opportunity together, choosing a field one can both love and live on.
Money matters, and pretending otherwise would be a disservice to students already anxious about their futures.
Practicality should inform the decision, not dictate it.
In conclusion, job availability is a factor to respect, not a rule to obey.
A field chosen purely for its job listings risks producing graduates who are good at nothing in particular and happy in nothing at all.
The happiest and most successful workers tend to be those who found the overlap between what they love and what the world will pay for.
Students should aim where their talents and interests meet real opportunity, rather than surrender the choice to a market that may well have moved on before they arrive.
